Or, at least, really reducing them? I was thinking about having a "free gas buffer" of, say, 200,000 gas per transaction that can be used only on opcodes that don't change state Basically, the only costs associated with e.g. an EIP-20 token transfer or swap would be the storage costs, not the computational costs Up to a point sounds like a great way to ddos low powered nodes higher gas has been discussed in the past, and Ethereum caters to users that want to run a full node on their laptop. So it does not matter if hardware can handle more load... it is held back by home users with laptops. Hi there, I just received word that EIP-3475 has been approved as a new standard (ERC-3475). Does that mean developers are now able to start developing and deploy tokens that conform to that standard right away? It's not a (core) EIP, it's just an ERC. Applications/smart contract stuff is not something discussed in this server, try https://ethereum-magicians.org/t/eip-3475-multiple-callable-bonds-standard/8691 or e.g. the CryptoDevs Discord. > sounds like a great way to ddos low powered nodes Definitely would have to be considered. ^ also would probably have at least some people design compute-heavy contracts to do it in chunks under 200k gas across multiple txs > ^ also would probably have at least some people design compute-heavy contracts to do it in chunks under 200k gas across multiple txs Here was what I considered: - Making it per transaction origin per transaction - Doesn't suffer from the below sybil attacks - Will make transactions perhaps too cheap (DDoS risk?) - Making it per transaction origin per [block/epoch] - People would just use multiple accounts to get around this - Making it per contract per transaction origin per [unit time] - Also suffers from the above sybil attack - Making it per contract per [unit time] - The gas would likely run out quickly on commonly-used contracts like Uniswap - Might encourage people to deploy many smaller contracts (Maybe a good thing due to sharding???) - Would mean that many commonly-used DApps would suddenly get re-engineered - How do you split this evenly among all the transactions? Instead of making it free couldn’t you make it a small fixed cost? It was a lump-sum "200k free non-state-changing gas per transaction" So it's effectively a negative fixed cost Yeah instead of free make it 1 gwei or something Aka charge a lower price for certain txs And reserve space for it in blocks seperate from the normal txs WDYM normal txs This would be for all transactions For opcodes that don’t change state I feel like Vitalik had a paper on this. Charging different gas fees based on demand for different types of txs. Yeh, at least separating storage and computation. But the "we need history and state expiry" and "zk-magic proving correctness of execution" play into all this as well I'm not talking about dynamically-priced opcodes. I'm talking about making them free unless you're doing something really complicated Or well Cheaper Not free (there's still always the EIP-1559 priority fee) But fundamentally someone could submit a transaction to the mempool with zero priority fee (for a grand total of zero gas fees) And maybe it would eventually go through Basically, with things like MEV-boost and the execution and consensus clients being split, it's no longer a good assumption that the cost of executing transactions that might be included in a block is split among all ethereum users why? If you have one execution client And 100 consensus clients using that execution client no, that's not possible. the other way around _maybe_, but generally it's 1-on-1 *furiously googles to see where the logic went wrong* The consensus client drives the execution client. It can hypothetically drive multiple, but you probably need some additional logic. And I also don't see why the number of execution clients would suddenly _decrease_, if anything it will increase I guess that's true Anyways, the other argument is that although it adds a deadweight loss economics-wise, it's "more than compensated for" in terms of UX (no more exorbitant prices) It'd just cause an imbalance in what ops/transactions are cheap, and which ones are not. I don't think it'd make L1 cheaper to use per se, just less transparent/fair, with what txs are effectively "prioritized".

excerpts.author: parithosh
excerpts.content:
You can also use nload and I think make it write to disk for later evaluation 😄

Or the approach I'd actually recommend: iperf3
Get a remote VPS, expose the required port and type in `iperf3 -s`
On your local machine, type `iperf3 -c <remote IP> -t 0` (unfortunately the timeout is 32bit, so this test can only run for 34 years)(switch the test to use UDP if your bandwidth is lower than what you expect, likely tcp overhead).

excerpts.author: pandapip1
excerpts.content:
> ^ also would probably have at least some people design compute-heavy contracts to do it in chunks under 200k gas across multiple txs 

Here was what I considered:
- Making it per transaction origin per transaction
  - Doesn't suffer from the below sybil attacks
  - Will make transactions perhaps too cheap (DDoS risk?)
- Making it per transaction origin per [block/epoch]
  - People would just use multiple accounts to get around this
- Making it per contract per transaction origin per [unit time]
  - Also suffers from the above sybil attack
- Making it per contract per [unit time]
  - The gas would likely run out quickly on commonly-used contracts like Uniswap
  - Might encourage people to deploy many smaller contracts (Maybe a good thing due to sharding???)
    - Would mean that many commonly-used DApps would suddenly get re-engineered
  - How do you split this evenly among all the transactions?
